\section{Introduction}\label{sec:introduction}

Reasoning models such as DeepSeek-R1~\cite{deepseekr1} and QwQ~\cite{qwq} have advanced language model capabilities by scaling chain-of-thought (CoT) inference, producing extended internal deliberation before generating final responses. These models interleave safety-aware reasoning with content generation across dozens of reasoning steps, and this very capacity for self-reflection introduces a new failure mode. Recent work has documented that reasoning models can ``self-jailbreak'': even without adversarial input modifications, the model's own CoT may transition from considering safety constraints to committing to produce harmful content~\cite{harmthoughts,selfjailbreak}. In such cases, the model's reasoning trace contains a \textbf{Safety Commitment Point} (CP), the first step after which safety reasoning permanently ceases and harmful generation proceeds unchecked. Detecting this transition in real time is essential for monitoring systems that must intervene before harmful content reaches users.

Existing safety detectors were designed for a different threat model. Methods based on hidden-state (HS) probing, such as TrajGuard~\cite{trajguard} and SafeSwitch~\cite{safeswitch}, monitor internal activations to classify adversarial inputs and achieve high accuracy (above 95\%) on standard Large Language Models (LLMs). Text-based monitors like SafeRemind~\cite{saferemind} and SafeThink~\cite{safethink} scan generated reasoning text for safety violations. Both families target external attacks on model inputs rather than the model's own internal commitment process. A fundamental question remains unanswered: when detecting safety commitment within multi-step reasoning, should a monitoring system read the model's hidden states or its generated text? Intuition suggests that HS features (4096 dimensions of internal computation) should be far more informative than text embeddings (384 dimensions from a sentence encoder). No prior work has tested this assumption systematically across models.

The two approaches rest on incompatible assumptions. Hidden-state probing~\cite{belinkov2019analysis} assumes that internal representations encode richer, earlier safety signals than externally visible text. Text monitoring assumes that the model's externalized reasoning already reveals its intent. Neither approach accounts for the temporal structure of multi-step reasoning, where commitment emerges gradually across steps rather than appearing as an instantaneous state change. Existing evaluations compare these modalities in isolation, on different models, with different metrics. No study has held all variables constant (same task, same models, same evaluation protocol) to measure whether modality selection actually matters for commitment detection.

We present the first systematic evaluation of safety commitment detection across three reasoning models (DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-8B, DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-32B, and QwQ-32B-Preview), two architectures (Llama, Qwen), and two parameter scales (8B, 32B). We compare HS probes, text monitors, temporal aggregation methods, and geometric baselines under identical conditions. Our central finding is counterintuitive: the choice between hidden states and text matters far less than the amount of temporal context provided to the detector. Expanding the observation window from $W{=}1$ to $W{=}25$ steps yields consistent gains confirmed across both modalities with complete window sweeps: +3.1 percentage points (pp) balanced accuracy, +12.9pp precision, and $-$4.8pp false positive rate (FPR) for HS probes, and +12.0pp accuracy, +23.2pp precision, $-$14.0pp FPR for text probes. Text probes benefit more from temporal context than HS probes, further confirming that the bottleneck is temporal rather than informational. On R1-8B, HS probes Pareto-dominate text probes (higher accuracy, precision, and lower FPR). On the 32B models, HS and text probes operate at different precision-FPR tradeoff points without clear dominance. This model-dependent result challenges the assumption that internal representations should uniformly dominate surface-level text for safety monitoring.

Our contributions are:
\begin{itemize}
    \item \textbf{Temporal context dominates modality choice.} Across three models and two signal modalities, temporal windowing (from $W{=}1$ to $W{=}25$) provides +3.1pp accuracy, +12.9pp precision, and $-$4.8pp FPR. Hidden states do not outperform text embeddings by the wide margin that information-theoretic reasoning would predict. The bottleneck in commitment detection is temporal, not informational.
    \item \textbf{The modality advantage is model-dependent.} On R1-8B, HS probes Pareto-dominate text probes: +8.4pp accuracy, +22.5pp precision, and 7pp lower FPR ($p{=}0.044$). On the two 32B models, HS and text probes operate at different precision-FPR tradeoff points without clear dominance (e.g., QwQ-32B text achieves lower FPR while HS achieves higher accuracy). Monitoring system design requires per-model validation rather than blanket modality assumptions.
    \item \textbf{Comprehensive negative results define method boundaries.} TrajGuard's Mahalanobis distance~\cite{trajguard} fails because safe and jailbreak trajectories occupy indistinguishable activation regions. Bayesian Online Change-Point Detection (BOCPD)~\cite{adams2007bayesian} and Cumulative Sum (CUSUM) fail because commitment is gradual rather than abrupt. Cross-model probe transfer fails entirely across all directions. Control task validation~\cite{hewitt2019control} confirms that probes capture genuine safety structure (selectivity 7.5--19pp above chance) rather than positional artifacts.
\end{itemize}

1	Large Language Models (LLMs) with Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning can self-jailbreak: their extended reasoning traces sometimes transition from safe deliberation to committed generation of harmful content. Detecting the precise moment of this safety commitment is essential for real-time intervention, yet no prior work has systematically compared hidden-state (HS) probes against text-based monitors for this task under controlled conditions. We present the first cross-model evaluation of temporal probing methods for safety commitment detection. Our study spans three reasoning models (DeepSeek-R1 8B/32B, QwQ-32B) across two architectures and two scales, and compares HS probes, text monitors, temporal windowing, Gated Recurrent Unit (GRU) sequence models, and geometric baselines including Mahalanobis distance, Bayesian Online Change Point Detection, and Cumulative Sum (CUSUM). First, temporal context is the dominant factor: expanding the observation window from 1 to 25 tokens improves precision by 12.9 percentage points and reduces false positive rate (FPR) across all models and modalities. Third, geometric change-point methods and cross-model transfer uniformly fail, and these negative results define clear boundaries of current approaches. Control tasks confirm that probes capture genuine safety-relevant structure rather than superficial distributional shifts.

\section{Responsible NLP Research Checklist}
\label{app:checklist}

We address the ARR Responsible NLP Research requirements below.

\begin{itemize}
    \item \textbf{Limitations discussed:} Yes (\cref{sec:limitations}).
    \item \textbf{Potential risks:} This research analyzes jailbreak traces to understand how reasoning models commit to generating harmful content. We do not develop new attack methods or release jailbreak prompts. All analyzed content comes from the publicly available HarmThoughts benchmark.
    \item \textbf{Computational budget:} Our experiments involve 3 models with 209, 100, and 95 traces respectively (404 total), using linear probes and single-layer GRUs. Total compute is minimal (under 2 GPU-hours on a single RTX A6000). No large-scale pretraining or finetuning was performed.
    \item \textbf{Data:} We use HarmThoughts, a publicly available benchmark with step-level safety annotations. No new data collection was performed.
    \item \textbf{Human subjects:} No human subjects research was conducted.
    \item \textbf{Reproducibility:} All hyperparameters are reported in \cref{app:gru_details,app:bocpd_config}. Code and corrected data will be released upon publication.
\end{itemize}


\section{Layer Sweep Results}
\label{app:layer_sweep}

For each model, we sweep all transformer layers and score each candidate layer using the product of balanced accuracy and crossing rate (accuracy-weighted layer selection, defined in \cref{sec:hs-probes}). This composite metric selects layers that simultaneously achieve good classification and reliable threshold crossing on jailbreak traces.

The selected layers are: R1-8B layer 14 (of 32 total, 44\% depth), R1-32B layer 24 (of 64, 37.5\% depth), and QwQ-32B layer 28 (of 64, 43.8\% depth). All three models concentrate safety-relevant information in the middle third of the network. Early layers (below 20\% depth) encode primarily syntactic features and score poorly on both accuracy and crossing rate. Final layers show high accuracy but low crossing rate, consistent with the hypothesis that late-layer representations encode safety state too close to output generation for early detection.

The optimal layer for R1-8B is notably shallow in absolute terms (layer 14), but this model has only 32 layers total. In relative depth, all three models converge to 37--44\%, suggesting a consistent architectural locus for safety commitment signals. Full per-layer results are available in supplementary materials.


\section{Window Size Ablation Details}
\label{app:window_ablation}

\cref{tab:window_full} reports the complete window size ablation across all three models and seven window sizes. The main text (\cref{sec:temporal_primary}) presents R1-8B results; here we provide the full data.

\begin{table}[h]
\centering
\small
\caption{Window size ablation: balanced accuracy, precision, pre-CP FPR (trace-level), and coverage ($K{=}1$) across all models. Best result per model in \textbf{bold}.}
\label{tab:window_full}
\begin{tabular}{llcccc}
\toprule
Model & $W$ & Bal. Acc. & Precision & FPR & Coverage \\
\midrule
\multirow{7}{*}{R1-8B}
 & 1  & 77.8 & 69.3 & 9.65 & 72.1 \\
 & 3  & 78.4 & 71.2 & 8.91 & 69.8 \\

\midrule
\multirow{7}{*}{R1-32B}
 & 1  & 72.1 & 58.4 & 12.3 & 68.5 \\

The optimal window size varies by model: R1-8B benefits from larger windows ($W{=}15$ onward), R1-32B peaks at $W{=}10$, and QwQ-32B reaches its optimum at $W{=}5$ before performance degrades. We hypothesize that this reflects differences in reasoning trace length: QwQ-32B produces shorter reasoning chains on average, so large windows incorporate irrelevant early steps that dilute the signal. R1-8B, with longer traces, benefits from the additional temporal smoothing that larger windows provide.

Across all models, the HS temporal improvement pattern is consistent: moving from $W{=}1$ to the model-specific optimum yields +3 to +4pp in balanced accuracy, +10 to +13pp in precision, and $-$3 to $-$5pp in FPR.

\subsection{Text Probe Window Ablation}
\label{app:text_window}

\cref{tab:text_window} reports the complete text probe window sweep on R1-8B, confirming that temporal context benefits text probes even more strongly than HS probes.

\begin{table}[h]
\centering
\caption{Text probe window ablation on R1-8B. Text probes gain +12.0pp accuracy from $W{=}1$ to $W{=}25$, compared to +3.1pp for HS probes over the same range. The larger marginal gain for text probes reflects their weaker single-step baseline.}
\label{tab:text_window}
\begin{tabular}{lcccc}
\toprule
$W$ & Bal. Acc. & Precision & FPR & Coverage \\
\midrule
 1  & 64.7 & 41.6 & 25.8 & 95.4 \\

\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

Text probes show monotonic improvement across all window sizes without the plateau observed in HS probes (which saturate around $W{=}15$). The absolute FPR reduction ($-$14.0pp) is nearly three times the HS reduction ($-$4.8pp), and accuracy gains (+12.0pp vs.\ +3.1pp) are four times larger. This asymmetry supports the interpretation that temporal context is the primary factor in commitment detection: text features, which encode less information per step, benefit proportionally more from observing the multi-step progression.


\section{GRU Training Details}
\label{app:gru_details}

\paragraph{Architecture.} We evaluate two GRU variants. The single-layer variant uses a GRU with hidden dimension 256, taking per-step hidden states from the best layer (selected by accuracy-weighted layer selection) as input. The multi-layer variant concatenates hidden states from 7 layers (evenly spaced through the network) at each step, producing a higher-dimensional input to the same GRU architecture.

\paragraph{Training procedure.} We train with Adam (learning rate $1 \times 10^{-3}$, default $\beta_1{=}0.9$, $\beta_2{=}0.999$), batch size 16, for a maximum of 50 epochs. Early stopping halts training when validation loss does not improve for 10 consecutive epochs. Input features are z-score normalized per dimension using training set statistics.

\paragraph{Evaluation.} We report crossing accuracy (the sustained accuracy at which the probe first exceeds chance for 5 consecutive steps) and detection lead (steps before CP at crossing point). All experiments use 3 random seeds; we report mean $\pm$ standard deviation.

\paragraph{Per-seed results for R1-8B (single-layer GRU).}

\begin{table}[h]
\centering
\small
\caption{R1-8B single-layer GRU results per seed. Lead is measured in steps before the commitment point.}
\label{tab:gru_seeds}
\begin{tabular}{lccc}
\toprule
Seed & Peak Acc. (\%) & Crossing Acc. (\%) & Lead (steps) \\
\midrule
1 & 85.2 & 74.3 & +4.8 \\
2 & 83.1 & 71.6 & +4.8 \\
3 & 83.4 & 70.4 & +0.9 \\
\midrule
Mean $\pm$ std & 83.9 $\pm$ 1.1 & 72.1 $\pm$ 2.0 & +3.5 $\pm$ 2.3 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

The high variance in lead time (standard deviation of 2.3 steps) is driven by seed 3, where the probe achieves good peak accuracy but crosses the detection threshold late. This variance underscores the sensitivity of early detection to initialization and motivates reporting per-seed results rather than relying on mean values alone.


\section{Control Task Methodology}
\label{app:control}

We follow the selectivity framework of \cite{hewitt2019control} to verify that our probes capture genuine safety-relevant structure rather than surface-level correlations.

\paragraph{Procedure.} For each model, we randomly permute the binary labels (pre-CP vs. post-CP) across all steps while preserving the marginal label distribution. We then retrain the probe with identical architecture (L2-regularized logistic regression) and hyperparameters on these shuffled labels. Selectivity is defined as:
\begin{equation}
    \text{Selectivity} = \text{Acc}_{\text{linguistic}} - \text{Acc}_{\text{control}}
\end{equation}
where $\text{Acc}_{\text{linguistic}}$ is the probe accuracy on true labels and $\text{Acc}_{\text{control}}$ is the accuracy on permuted labels. A selectivity of zero indicates that the probe exploits only non-linguistic features (e.g., position); higher values confirm that the representation encodes task-relevant information.

\paragraph{Results.} We repeat the control experiment 5 times with different random permutations and report the mean control accuracy. Selectivity scores are: R1-8B 12.5pp (layer 14), QwQ-32B 18.9pp (layer 2), R1-32B 7.5pp (corrected layer 10). All values exceed the 5pp threshold recommended by \cite{hewitt2019control} as evidence of genuine linguistic encoding, though R1-32B's weaker selectivity is consistent with its overall weaker hidden-state signal.

\paragraph{Position-only baseline.} As a complementary validation, we train a logistic regression classifier using only the normalized step index ($t / T$ where $T$ is the total trace length) as the input feature. This baseline tests whether temporal position alone explains probe performance. On R1-8B, the position-only baseline produces 15.8\% FPR compared to 8.1\% for the HS probe at matched detection rates. The probe's substantially lower FPR confirms that hidden state features carry information beyond what step position provides.


\section{BOCPD/CUSUM Configuration Sweep}
\label{app:bocpd_config}

We sweep hyperparameters for both Bayesian Online Change-Point Detection (BOCPD) and Cumulative Sum (CUSUM) methods applied to the temporal probe score sequences.

\paragraph{BOCPD configurations.} BOCPD models the sequence of probe scores as piecewise-constant segments with Gaussian observation noise. The hazard rate $\lambda$ controls the prior probability of a change-point at each step ($P(\text{change}) = 1/\lambda$).

\paragraph{CUSUM configurations.} CUSUM accumulates evidence for a positive mean shift. The drift parameter $\delta$ sets the minimum shift size to detect, and the threshold $h$ controls the detection boundary.

\begin{table}[h]
\centering
\small
\caption{Change-point method configuration sweep on R1-8B. Detection rate is the fraction of jailbreak traces where the method fires. Lead is measured in steps before CP. Simple threshold baseline included for comparison.}
\label{tab:cpd_sweep}
\begin{tabular}{llcc}
\toprule
Method & Configuration & Det. Rate (\%) & Lead (steps) \\
\midrule
\multirow{5}{*}{BOCPD}
 & $\lambda = 5$   & 97 & +2.1 \\
 & $\lambda = 10$  & 93 & +3.5 \\
 & $\lambda = 20$  & 87 & +4.2 \\
 & $\lambda = 50$  & 72 & +5.8 \\
 & $\lambda = 100$ & 58 & +7.1 \\
\midrule
\multirow{9}{*}{CUSUM}
 & $\delta{=}0.5$, $h{=}3$ & 89 & +1.4 \\
 & $\delta{=}0.5$, $h{=}5$ & 76 & +2.3 \\
 & $\delta{=}0.5$, $h{=}8$ & 61 & +3.1 \\
 & $\delta{=}1.0$, $h{=}3$ & 82 & +1.1 \\
 & $\delta{=}1.0$, $h{=}5$ & 68 & +1.9 \\
 & $\delta{=}1.0$, $h{=}8$ & 52 & +2.7 \\
 & $\delta{=}2.0$, $h{=}3$ & 71 & +0.8 \\
 & $\delta{=}2.0$, $h{=}5$ & 54 & +1.5 \\
 & $\delta{=}2.0$, $h{=}8$ & 38 & +2.1 \\
\midrule
Simple threshold & $\tau = 0.5$ & 91 & +4.9 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

The best BOCPD configuration ($\lambda{=}10$) achieves 93\% detection rate with +3.5 steps lead. The simple threshold baseline achieves comparable detection (91\%) with superior lead (+4.9 steps). All CUSUM configurations underperform the simple threshold on lead time, and most also show lower detection rates.

These results confirm that probe score transitions toward unsafe reasoning are gradual rather than abrupt. Change-point methods assume a sharp distributional shift; the actual transition is a smooth drift that a fixed threshold detects earlier. The practical recommendation is that simple thresholding on temporal probe scores is preferable to more complex sequential detection methods for this task.


\section{M002 Bug Disclosure}
\label{app:bug}

We disclose a bug discovered during development that affected intermediate results for QwQ-32B.

\paragraph{Issue.} In experiment M002 (text baseline evaluation), the QwQ-32B text probe was inadvertently initialized with a midpoint heuristic placeholder rather than true sentence embeddings from all-MiniLM-L6-v2. The two modalities show no meaningful difference on QwQ-32B, consistent with the non-significant results on R1-32B.
